prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, bringing atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Reading the eight ballots, B015 is the only shortlisted candidate that every one of us ranked, and it is also the one where I am most confident about the physics. The magic-wavelength idea is a clear conceptual step: choose the lattice wavelength so that the light shift cancels for the clock transition, and a large number of atoms can be interrogated at once without Doppler or recoil broadening. What followed is quantitative atomic physics of the kind I respect, with every systematic shift (blackbody radiation, lattice hyperpolarisability, collisions, spin-exchange) identified, modelled and measured, and agreement between independent clocks at the 10^-18 level in JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and elsewhere. This is not one measurement that nobody has repeated. It also yields real science: tests of the constancy of fundamental constants, gravitational redshift across millimetres inside a single cloud, and a clear path to a new definition of the second. Katori's proposal and first demonstrations and Ye's drive to record accuracy and many-body clock physics make a clean two-person attribution, which is rare on this list.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection, which I take seriously because I am an atomic physicist and might be too fond of it, is that this can be read as an extended programme of engineering refinement on top of two earlier prizes (frequency combs in 2005, ion control and ion clocks in 2012) rather than as a discovery that tells us something unexpected about nature. I would answer that the magic-wavelength concept is itself the new idea and that the precision opens new physics, but I admit that the case is one of invention and measurement rather than surprise. A second reservation is that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, and ion clocks (Al+, Yb+) compete at similar accuracy, so a citation must not overstate which platform is 'the' clock. Contributions such as Lemonde's early work and the many-body spin-exchange studies are outside the credited names.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B015 first for the same reasons of measurement quality, notes the lattice contribution is distinct from the 2005 comb prize, and raises whether ion-clock work (Wineland, Rosenband) should be credited too.
responses.response: I agree on the measurement case and on the distinction from the comb prize, but I disagree with widening the credit to ion clocks. Wineland was recognised in 2012 for controlling single quantum systems, and the ion-clock story belongs to that lineage. Adding Rosenband or similar names would blur a clean two-person attribution and push us above the three-name limit when we want a tidy citation. I would keep the citation specific to lattice clocks and let the ion-clock programme stand as context.

responses.point: Pearce puts IceCube (B014) first as an instrument-builder's new observational window and ranks B015 second, while noting that the 2005 and 2012 prizes may make the clocks look incremental.
responses.response: I take the incremental concern seriously, but I think the distinction is real: combs gave a way to count optical cycles, and the lattice clock is a separate idea about how to hold many atoms without perturbing the transition. On IceCube I defer to you and Ulf Danielsson on astroparticle physics, and the diffuse flux is clearly a discovery by nature. My hesitation is attribution, since you and others note that AMANDA, DUMAND, Baikal and a collaboration of hundreds stand behind two names, and only two sources (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) are individually significant. B015 is simpler to credit and independently reproduced already, so I would put it ahead, though I would not call B014 unreasonable as the alternative.

responses.point: Olsson ranks topological insulators and the quantum anomalous Hall effect (B003) first as a theory-plus-two-experiments case with fifteen years of replication, and ranks B015 third.
responses.response: I agree that B003 has strong maturity and a very large conceptual footprint, and I ranked the related B018 only seventh because I am not equipped to judge condensed-matter priority, not because I doubt the physics. My worry is attribution: Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Mele and Hasan all have substantial claims, Zhang has died, and B003 and B018 split the credit differently, so the committee would be choosing among overlapping three-person sets. Also the 2016 prize already honoured topological phases, which weakens the novelty somewhat. If the committee's view is that topology deserves a second prize, I would want the Kane, Mele, Molenkamp question settled before I could support it over B015.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B039) first as a foundational new regime of strong coupling in a circuit, while flagging overlap with the 2025 prize and his own closeness to these groups.
responses.response: I agree that circuit QED is a clean new regime and I placed it fourth. My difficulty is timing: the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is only a year old, and a second superconducting-circuit prize so soon seems hard to justify when the platform has partly engineering character. I also note and respect your own disclosure of proximity to these groups, which suggests you may wish to be careful in the final stage. I list B039 as an alternative because the theory-plus-experiment story for Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf is good, but I would not pick it now.

responses.point: Mehlig puts fluctuation theorems (B005) first as an exact, universal result with a simple mechanism and about 25 years of experimental confirmation, and places B015 sixth.
responses.response: I appreciate the appeal of an exact statement, and I agree the Jarzynski and Crooks relations are beautiful and widely verified. However, the attribution you yourself describe is the problem: Gallavotti and Cohen, Kurchan, Lebowitz and Spohn and Hatano and Sasa all have claims, and the credited trio omits several. A prize that resolves that priority dispute with three names will be criticised for years. Only you rank it, and it has no support among the others, so I cannot see it becoming the preferred configuration, though I accept your point that conceptual understanding matters as much as technology.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads the optical lattice clock as one discovery or as a long programme of refinements following earlier prizes on frequency combs and ion control.
How to word the citation so it does not imply that lattice clocks alone, rather than also single-ion clocks, define the state of the art in timekeeping.
Exact priority between Katori's proposal and first demonstrations, and contributions by Lemonde and others, which I have not independently verified.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second makes this the right year or means the committee should wait.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict specific to Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile. I should flag that I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with Ursula Keller's group, and my own work includes precision atomic theory, so I am professionally close to this field, but neither Katori nor Ye appears among my listed collaborators.
